title: Tuna vs Salmon: Protein, Omega-3, Fat and Calories

seo.title: Tuna vs Salmon: Protein, Omega-3 and Calories
seo.meta_description: Yellowfin tuna is leaner and packs more protein per calorie; salmon provides far more EPA and DHA. Mercury varies substantially by tuna species.
seo.search_intent: Compare tuna and salmon on protein, fat, omega-3, calories and mercury without treating all tuna as one species.

excerpt: Tuna and salmon are two very different ways to get protein. Per 100 grams cooked, yellowfin tuna has roughly 29 grams of protein and 130 calories, while Atlantic salmon is closer to 22 grams and 200–210 calories. Salmon's advantage shows up elsewhere: it provides far more EPA and DHA. Mercury in tuna also depends heavily on the species.
content_html:
Tuna and salmon often get grouped together as two high-protein fish, but nutritionally they do not do exactly the same job. Lean fresh tuna packs a lot of protein into very few calories; salmon provides less protein per calorie, but an amount of omega-3 that yellowfin tuna does not come close to matching.

If the priority is protein with very few calories, tuna has the edge. If you want EPA and DHA, salmon wins by a wide margin. And once mercury enters the discussion, the tuna species matters.

Start with a like-for-like comparison

To keep packing oil, added sodium and draining from muddying the picture, it helps to begin with cooked fresh fish: yellowfin tuna versus Atlantic salmon.

Per 100 g cookedYellowfin tunaAtlantic salmon
Calories~130~205
Protein~29 g~22 g
Fat~0.6 g~12 g
EPA + DHA~0.1–0.2 g~2.1 g

The protein gap is real, but it is not the most striking part: tuna provides about 7 extra grams per 100 grams. The much larger contrast is fat and omega-3. In this example, salmon can supply more than ten times as much EPA+DHA.

Tuna packs protein unusually efficiently

With less than 1 gram of fat per 100 grams, almost all of yellowfin tuna's calories come from protein. About 5 ounces can provide roughly 40 grams of protein for around 180 calories. That is a very high protein-to-calorie ratio.

Reaching a similar amount of protein with Atlantic salmon takes about 6 ounces. That serving is closer to 350–370 calories because it also provides roughly 20 grams of fat.

But salmon's fat is part of the reason to eat it

Calories alone would make the comparison incomplete. Salmon contains substantial amounts of EPA and DHA, the long-chain marine omega-3 fats. NIH data list about 1.83 grams of EPA+DHA in 3 ounces of cooked farmed Atlantic salmon.

The same amount of cooked yellowfin tuna is around 0.10 gram. In other words, salmon is higher in fat, but a meaningful part of that difference is exactly what gives it the omega-3 advantage.

For mercury, “tuna” is too broad a label

FDA/EPA places canned light tuna in the Best Choices category, albacore/white and yellowfin tuna in Good Choices, and bigeye tuna in Choices to Avoid for people covered by the pregnancy and child fish-advice chart. Salmon is a Best Choice.

FDA commercial-fish data show the scale: canned light tuna averages about 0.13 ppm mercury, albacore and yellowfin about 0.35 ppm, bigeye about 0.69 ppm, and fresh or frozen salmon about 0.02 ppm.

So if mercury matters in the decision, the species and product matter more than the generic word “tuna.”

Canned tuna deserves a separate comparison

Canned light tuna in water is not nutritionally identical to albacore, yellowfin or tuna packed in oil. Species, packing liquid, draining, fat, calories and sodium can all change.

Canned light tuna also tends to be lower in mercury than albacore. Using the numbers from a fresh yellowfin steak to describe every can of tuna would therefore mix unlike products.

So which one should you choose?

There is no need to force a single winner. Lean tuna is excellent when you want a lot of protein for few calories; salmon provides less protein per calorie but far more EPA and DHA and is generally low in mercury.

In a real diet, rotating the two along with other fish usually makes more sense than treating this as a permanent either-or choice.

faq.question: Which has more protein, tuna or salmon?
faq.answer: Cooked yellowfin tuna has about 29 g/100 g versus roughly 22 g/100 g in Atlantic salmon.

faq.question: Which has more omega-3?
faq.answer: Salmon by a very large margin for EPA and DHA: roughly 2 g/100 g versus about 0.1–0.2 g in cooked yellowfin tuna.

faq.question: Does tuna have more mercury than salmon?
faq.answer: Many tuna species and products do, but the amount varies substantially. Canned light tuna is lower than albacore or yellowfin, while bigeye is much higher; salmon is typically low.
